stances.claim: The 1987 Charter framers, traumatized by martial-rule repression and tyranny, deliberately designed an anti-authoritarian Constitution by reducing presidential powers, strengthening Congress and independent agencies, and -- most importantly -- giving the judiciary overarching grave-abuse-of-discretion powers to subdue executive and legislative abuses, making the PH SC the most powerful tribunal in the world, more so than even the US SC.

The SC corrects itself when convinced by incontrovertible facts -- LAMP (April 24 2012) unanimously upheld PDAF, then Belgica (Nov 10 2013) unanimously struck it down a year later -- demonstrating the Court's capacity for self-correction.

The Court's asymmetric TRO treatment -- immediate TRO on MOA-AD signing day but no TRO on the functionally-equivalent Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro, and no TRO on EDCA despite the Charter's explicit Senate-concurrence requirement for foreign military bases/troops/facilities -- raises questions about consistency, though Panganiban does not push this into open criticism.

The Constitution is a living instrument that should be interpreted according to the evolving needs of the people who ratified it, not rigidly according to its letter -- and with this mindset the SC can be the anchor of the ship of state during stormy times.
stances.confidence: asserted as Panganiban's preferred interpretive philosophy

notable_anecdotes: Reader Mongontawar Gubat's rueful joke that Filipino lawyers and policemen can hardly memorize the Miranda rights -- 'Sa porsiento ka na lang magpaliwanag' (Just explain it on the percentage [i.e., share of the takings]) -- the rare instance of CJP quoting a reader's wry Tagalog quip about systemic corruption of arrest procedures.

The framing of Miranda rights as US-SC-invented but written into the Philippine Charter's text -- a reversal of the usual US-influence-on-PH-jurisprudence narrative, here PH outdoes the US by Charter-codifying what the US handles only by judicial decision.

The MOA-AD vs FAB asymmetric TRO treatment -- same provisions, opposite SC response -- quietly invoked without explicit criticism, the kind of empirical observation CJP raises but lets stand for the reader.

The Court is the most powerful tribunal in the world claim -- anchored not in jurisdictional reach but in the GAD-duty being unparalleled even in the US SC, the doctrinal anchor for the entire FLP-judicial-power thesis.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that the 1987 Constitution -- drafted in record one year by handpicked-not-elected Cory Aquino framers traumatized by martial-rule repression -- was deliberately designed to make authoritarian rule impossible by reducing presidential powers, strengthening Congress and the independent agencies, writing a detailed-and-lengthy Charter contrary to the broad-brief-definite tradition, and most importantly giving the judiciary overarching grave-abuse-of-discretion powers undefined by the Charter and left for the SC to flesh out, making the Philippine SC the most powerful tribunal in the world, more so than even the US SC. He notes the framers wrote into the Charter text Miranda rights that the US handles only by SC decision (with reader Mongontawar Gubat's rueful 'Sa porsiento ka na lang magpaliwanag' joke on systemic memorization failure), and that illegally-obtained evidence and forced confessions are inadmissible, sometimes acquitting the factually guilty. He praises the Court's capacity for self-correction -- LAMP (April 24 2012) unanimously upheld PDAF, Belgica (Nov 10 2013) unanimously struck it down a year later -- while raising without pressing the asymmetric TRO treatment of MOA-AD (TRO'd on signing day) versus the functionally equivalent FAB (no TRO) and EDCA (no TRO despite the Charter's Senate-concurrence requirement for foreign military bases/troops/facilities). He closes with his living-Constitution interpretive philosophy: the Charter should be construed according to the evolving needs of the people who ratified it, not rigidly according to its letter, and with this mindset the SC can use its vast powers to speed up justice, minimize technicalities, and be the anchor of the ship of state during stormy times.
